purpose: Finished English focus-description overrides for the 50 V5 named-country offer focuses and 12 personnel-policy focuses. Effects, focus structure and localized titles remain unchanged.

focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_gaullist_gre_01: Greek orders for the Mirage F1 show how a French-designed aircraft can serve a partner without merging its armed forces with ours. Paris can now offer maintenance courses and a common supply standard, helping both air services keep their aircraft available. French technicians and fuel savings come at the cost of training commitments and export terms that Athens must find worthwhile.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_gaullist_rom_02: The Renault-Dacia licence brought French engineering into Romanian production while leaving assembly on Romanian soil. A new vehicle-parts arrangement can extend that practical exchange to utility transport, giving French suppliers a wider market and our plants access to useful components. The bargain asks both governments to share standards and accept licensing limits; Romania remains free to refuse or set its own terms.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_gaullist_ger_03: Airbus and the Alpha Jet show that French and West German engineers can divide the work on advanced aircraft while preserving separate national services. A further airframe programme would pool skills, orders and training capacity. France would gain a broader industrial base, but shared tooling and export decisions would limit the freedom to direct every production choice from Paris.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_gaullist_eng_04: Concorde and Jaguar demonstrate the reach of Anglo-French aerospace cooperation, from civil flight to combat aviation. France can propose regular integration courses for crews and ground teams, improving safe operation of shared systems and preserving hard-won technical experience. The courses require specialist personnel and a continuing budget; they do not give either government authority over the other's deployments.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_gaullist_sov_05: French and Soviet space cooperation has already opened a channel for peaceful scientific work. Paris can propose reciprocal instrumentation missions that apply precision measurement to civilian space and industrial research, while keeping strategic weapons programmes outside the exchange. The work strengthens technical capacity over time and requires sustained education spending; it also asks France to manage scientific openness without weakening its independent defence.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_orthodox_gaullist_sov_06: The 1970 Franco-Soviet consultation and later cooperation declarations provide room for practical scientific contacts despite the divide between our systems. A bounded programme in civilian measurement and industrial research can improve French technical productivity while maintaining the force de frappe under national authority. The arrangement carries an education cost and demands care over sensitive knowledge, but neither side need surrender its strategic independence.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_orthodox_gaullist_eng_07: Britain's independent deterrent and France's own force must remain under separate national authority. Paris can nevertheless invite British naval staffs to compare undersea procedures, navigation and fleet support, improving the professional knowledge available to both services. Such consultation carries a personnel cost and builds habits of cooperation, but it neither combines the deterrents nor delegates nuclear release decisions.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_orthodox_gaullist_ger_08: Franco-German defence consultations and later exercises offer a basis for closer work on conventional crisis procedures. Paris can propose shared staff education and mobilization practice while keeping French units under French command. Better reinforcement planning takes time, instructors and public funds; the protocol would improve coordination with Bonn without creating an integrated army or any transfer of nuclear authority.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_orthodox_gaullist_gre_09: Greek orders for French Mirage aircraft established a commercial relationship between an independent air force and a French supplier. Paris can invite Athens into a standing maintenance and supply convention that lowers the burden of keeping French aircraft available and gives both air services dependable technical support. The arrangement requires public funding and Greek agreement, while leaving Greece free to choose its suppliers and operational policy.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_orthodox_gaullist_usa_10: The Ailleret-Lemnitzer arrangements showed how France could coordinate with the Atlantic Alliance while retaining national command. A regular deconfliction channel with Washington can extend that practice through staff education and planning for conventional contingencies. French officers gain access to allied experience, but training requires public expenditure and close attention to sovereignty; no French unit is placed under foreign command by this consultation.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_liberal_ger_11: The Alpha Jet and Airbus programmes show how French and West German firms can share specialised production while keeping distinct national forces. Paris can invite German avionics suppliers into a reciprocal standards and component arrangement, improving access to aircraft and command equipment. Training and outside supplier links carry costs, however, and France must balance competition and export access against the wish to retain a wholly domestic design chain.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_liberal_eng_12: The Jaguar programme and civil-aircraft collaboration have given British and French manufacturers experience in common certification. A reciprocal export accord could help firms navigate each other's standards and reach customers beyond the Channel. French suppliers would gain commercial access, but concessions to foreign competition and tax incentives have a public price. The accord creates neither a shared government nor a common arms-export policy.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_liberal_usa_13: Rambouillet-era economic dialogue and growing computer industries make a civilian computing exchange a practical next step. French and American engineers could compare standards and industrial applications, helping laboratories and manufacturers improve productivity. The programme requires investment in education and exposes French firms to stronger outside influence over technical choices. Its purpose is civilian computing and industrial practice, not military command integration or the transfer of sensitive weapons systems.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_liberal_hol_14: The Common Market has made investment between France and the Netherlands a regular political concern. Paris can propose a bilateral clearance channel that gives firms clearer routes to seek capital while preserving each country's fiscal authority. French enterprises gain access to additional investment, but tax concessions reduce public receipts and Dutch participation depends on its own government's decision. Both states retain control of wider monetary policy.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_centre_bel_15: French and Belgian authorities already work across a busy border shaped by common European institutions. Paris can invite Belgium into a depot and emergency-services compact that aligns procedures for moving supplies, repairing infrastructure and supporting civil protection in a crisis. The arrangement improves resilience and staff training, but requires continuing public coordination and compatible standards. Belgium retains control of its services and decides its priorities.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_centre_ger_16: French and West German officers have developed channels for consultation as both states rebuild practical defence cooperation. Paris can propose reciprocal staff courses in conventional doctrine, mobilization and command education, strengthening professional ties without combining the armies. The programme needs instructors and a continuing education budget; its value lies in shared understanding, while French political and nuclear decisions remain entirely national.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_centre_ita_17: France and Italy share Mediterranean sea lanes and a practical interest in safe escort operations. Paris can invite Italian crews and staff to conventional courses in navigation, communications and fleet coordination. Better naval doctrine takes sustained training and higher personnel commitments, but does not require a joint fleet or guarantee of intervention. Rome decides whether the courses serve Italian interests, just as France retains its own command.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_centre_eng_18: British and French shipyards have a history of industrial exchange, while both navies depend on reliable Atlantic and Channel routes. Paris can propose common workshop standards for maritime equipment, supporting dockyard capacity and maintenance knowledge. Investment in naval production draws resources away from land factories, and an agreement would require mutually acceptable specifications. The proposal offers cooperation on conventional industry without binding either fleet to the other's orders.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_radical_bel_19: Local authorities on both sides of the Franco-Belgian border face shared problems of roads, water, repair and emergency access. Paris can invite Belgian public engineers into reciprocal planning and workshop exchanges, improving infrastructure repair and construction practice. The programme requires technical staff and public education, but gives practical responsibilities to local services rather than creating a central European authority. Belgian participation remains a sovereign choice.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_radical_swi_20: Swiss precision instruments and French public laboratories offer complementary strengths for measuring energy use and industrial performance. A reciprocal applied-research network could reduce waste while widening the reach of civilian engineering. The work needs sustained education and research funds, and the gains depend on open technical exchange rather than immediate production orders. Switzerland would choose whether to participate; the programme assumes no military alignment or change to either country's institutions.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_radical_ita_21: Italian and French engineers can compare the practical demands of territorial transport, road repair and reserve services. Paris can propose courses that prepare technicians to keep vehicles and supply routes serviceable during emergencies. Shared training reduces logistical strain but requires instructors and continuing public investment. Each government keeps its own command, while the exchange concentrates on emergency logistics and public engineering.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_radical_spr_22: Spain's developing regional framework offers a later model for cooperation among local authorities. France can propose an exchange on road maintenance, public works and infrastructure repair, building practical ties without deciding Spain's place in Europe. Technical education and staff time carry a real cost, but the benefits reach beyond central administrations. Madrid would choose its terms; the agreement neither grants nor requires membership in the Common Market.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_socialist_ger_23: Airbus and later conventional defence projects show that French and West German industries can share work while their armed forces remain under separate command. A reciprocal staff and airframe compact would strengthen technical training and access to multirole aircraft components. France would pay for education and accept some dependence on shared suppliers. The arrangement supports conventional readiness without handing Bonn authority over French deployments or the national deterrent.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_socialist_eng_24: A rapid-action establishment depends on staff who can plan, supply and recover units as well as on troops ready to move. Paris can invite British officers to reciprocal courses in logistics and operational coordination, improving French readiness and organizational experience. The programme raises the cost of maintaining professional personnel and requires Britain to agree to its scope. It grants no foreign access, troop deployment or intervention authority.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_socialist_alg_25: The 1982 Franco-Algerian gas agreement exposed the political bargain behind energy supply: reliable deliveries could support French industry, while public investment and industrial commitments carried costs for both countries. Paris can propose technical cooperation on efficient use and industrial skills rather than treating gas as a free resource. The programme supports French productivity, but requires education and investment and leaves Algeria free to negotiate its own commercial terms.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_socialist_ser_26: The 1966 France-Yugoslavia scientific agreement established a channel for reciprocal research programmes. Paris can use that relationship to propose applied engineering courses for industrial conversion and civilian production, connecting French laboratories with Yugoslav technical institutions. The exchange can raise productivity and skills, but education requires public funding and conversion means choosing civilian orders over immediate arms expansion. Belgrade would determine whether the proposed industrial scope fits its own plans.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_communist_sov_27: The 1975 Franco-Soviet declaration opened formal cooperation in industrial, scientific and technical fields. A public-industry standards mission could let French and Soviet plants compare methods for organizing production and training workers. This would improve line coordination while demanding education investment and accepting slower efficiency gains during transition. The exchange stays within civilian industry: it neither brings France into the Warsaw Pact nor transfers command of French forces.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_communist_ddr_28: The 1973 France-GDR technical agreement provides a civilian basis for exchanging machine-tool practice. Paris can propose a further signals-equipment workshop programme, extending industrial methods into a dual-use field by mutual agreement. French equipment costs and technical training benefit, but standards become more dependent on a foreign supplier network. The initiative does not imply Pact membership, military command transfer or a guaranteed East German commitment.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_communist_ita_29: Public enterprises and repair services in France and Italy can compare how to keep industrial equipment working and preserve skilled employment. Paris can propose a reciprocal workshop network inspired by the public-sector and Eurocommunist debates of the period, without assuming that Italy's government shares the PCF's outlook. Repair capacity improves at the cost of continuing social commitments; Rome remains free to accept, decline or shape the arrangement.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_communist_alg_30: Franco-Algerian cartographic cooperation and agricultural training offer concrete foundations for technical exchange. Paris can propose linking survey teams with vocational schools, improving maps, engineering skills and local agricultural infrastructure. The programme requires instructors and equipment, but builds practical capacity without a military alignment. Algeria's institutions would set their own priorities, and the partnership would extend existing civilian cooperation rather than dictate production or political choices.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_old_guard_sov_31: A hard-line French government can seek staff courses and maintenance instruction from the Soviet Union while reserving command of French units to Paris. The exchange would deepen professional ties and strengthen doctrine, but require sustained education spending and increase exposure to Soviet standards. An explicit political agreement would precede any staff mission; France's command and deterrent remain national responsibilities.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_old_guard_ddr_32: The 1973 France-GDR agreement dealt with industrial and technical cooperation, not shared military production. A French hard-line government could now propose common workshops for standard-series equipment, extending machine-tool exchange into defence by consent. Repetition would improve output consistency, while training costs and fixed designs reduce flexibility. The East German government retains its own authority over participation and any military standards it is willing to discuss.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_old_guard_rom_33: The Renault-Dacia licensing relationship shows how French design and Romanian assembly can serve both industries without requiring political alignment. Paris can propose reciprocal workshops for utility vehicles and domestic parts, strengthening civilian productivity and making equipment more affordable. Licensing terms and tax concessions limit the gains, and Bucharest retains control over production decisions. The offer extends a commercial precedent; it does not presume Romanian adherence to a French programme.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_old_guard_ser_34: France and Yugoslavia have maintained a technical cooperation channel since 1966. Paris can use it to develop an independent civilian research programme with Yugoslav institutions, expanding skills and industrial knowledge without copying Soviet standards. Education takes time and public resources, while the political value rests on non-aligned cooperation. Belgrade may set the limits of its participation, and the arrangement leaves French command and procurement authority national.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_psu_ser_35: Yugoslav worker self-management and the France-Yugoslavia science agreement offer distinct precedents for cooperative workshops. Paris can propose exchanges between worker-managed enterprises, technical schools and French public firms, testing whether local control can improve production without losing reliability. The experiment brings continuing social costs and may reduce peak efficiency. Belgrade would negotiate its participation; the programme does not assume Yugoslav institutions can simply be transplanted into France.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_psu_alg_36: French support for Algerian agricultural education and the bilateral mapping convention show how technical schools can serve practical local needs. Paris can propose reciprocal courses in survey work, infrastructure maintenance and vocational training. Both countries gain skilled personnel, but instructors and equipment must be funded and directed toward civilian priorities. Algerian schools would shape the curriculum; this partnership offers capacity-building rather than a military relationship or imposed development plan.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_psu_swi_37: The Alpine frontier makes rescue, repair and civil protection a practical concern for France and Switzerland. Paris can propose a civic-service protocol for local repair teams, emergency workshops and shared training, building resilience through civilian cooperation. The arrangement needs trained personnel and a continuing service commitment, drawing resources away from the professional force. Bern would agree the scope, and any assistance would be requested by the affected government.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_psu_ger_38: French and West German research institutions can work together on civilian instrumentation, including water measurement and industrial energy use. A reciprocal programme would improve technical knowledge while preserving separate national choices on armaments. Education costs remain substantial, and both states must agree on what information their laboratories share. The agreement strengthens civilian science without requiring a common defence policy.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_ecology_ger_39: The International Commission for the Protection of the Rhine, founded in 1950, and the 1976 pollution conventions show that river protection depends on sustained cross-border monitoring. France can propose joint measurement and infrastructure planning with West Germany, reducing energy waste while supporting public works. The programme requires laboratories, trained staff and agreement on standards. It offers a practical environmental settlement without claiming that one government can dictate the other's industrial policy.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_ecology_swi_40: France and Switzerland share Alpine roads, watersheds and emergency routes that require reliable maintenance. Paris can propose a bilateral service for infrastructure repair, rescue logistics and practical training, giving local authorities a way to coordinate across the border. The programme needs skilled crews and an ongoing personnel commitment. Bern retains control of its services, and assistance would follow an explicit request from the affected authorities.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_ecology_eng_41: The 1969 Bonn Agreement already gives North Sea states a framework for pollution surveillance, research, exercises and requested assistance. France and Britain can strengthen practical work against oil pollution in the Channel, coordinating repair teams and training without turning environmental cooperation into a military pact. Technical courses and maintenance have a public cost, but shared standards help both governments respond faster when coastal infrastructure is threatened.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_ecology_nry_42: Norway and France share interests in safer offshore industry and cleaner northern waters. The Ekofisk blowout demonstrated how industrial accidents cross borders, while the Bonn framework provides a regional precedent for monitoring and assistance. Paris can propose reciprocal research on energy safety and efficient industrial practice. The work requires specialist education and negotiated access to data, while Oslo retains control of its resources and industrial policy.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_cid_bel_43: The CID's 1970 calls for independent commerce and craft credit provide a domestic constituency for this proposal. Paris can invite Belgium to discuss a workshop-credit channel that helps small firms finance tools and cross-border contracts. Such access may encourage investment, but tax concessions reduce public receipts and Brussels need not adopt French business rules. The agreement applies to willing enterprises; it does not reorganize Belgian institutions or markets.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_cid_swi_44: Independent workshops on both sides of the French-Swiss border can share repair methods and apprenticeship placements. Paris can propose an accord that helps small firms maintain utility equipment and train skilled workers without depending on a large national contractor. Lower equipment costs come with education commitments and uneven supplier capacity. Swiss participation would be voluntary, and the programme gives local enterprises room to negotiate their own contracts.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_cid_ita_45: Artisan firms can supply specialised components when public contracts use clear specifications and reliable payment. Paris can invite Italian workshops into a reciprocal supplier convention that spreads orders among smaller producers and supports infantry and communications equipment. Tax concessions and fragmented output carry a price, and both governments must agree on standards before firms invest. The agreement gives independent producers a voice in procurement without centralizing every contract.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_cid_spr_46: Rural suppliers and independent traders can help France and Spain maintain equipment and local services beyond the largest industrial centres. Paris can propose a voluntary exchange of agricultural tools, office equipment and supplier expertise, giving small firms new opportunities while supporting rural productivity. Tax concessions reduce public income, and the programme asks both governments to coordinate contracts without changing Spanish institutions, borders or market law.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_national_gre_47: Greek orders for the Mirage in 1974 and 1985 show that French aircraft can succeed in a foreign national service. Paris can propose a supplier convention with Athens that strengthens maintenance and aircraft availability while favouring French contracts. The arrangement reduces production costs but gives up some public revenue; it depends on Greek consent and leaves Greece in full control of its aircraft and operations.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_national_rom_48: The Renault-Dacia licensing relationship offers a commercial example of French engineering adapted for Romanian production. Paris can propose a renewed vehicle-licensing channel that supports domestic assembly and access to utility equipment without requiring political alignment. The contract depends on agreed royalties, suppliers and production standards, and tax concessions reduce French receipts. Bucharest remains sovereign over its industry and may negotiate different terms or decline the offer.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_national_eng_49: The National Front's 1973 platform sought priority political agreement with Britain on defence coordination. Paris can propose reciprocal staff education focused on conventional planning and naval doctrine, improving French expertise while keeping command and nuclear release decisions national. Training raises personnel costs, and London decides whether the arrangement fits British policy. The two governments retain sovereign control over deployments and strategic forces.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_v5_national_ger_50: The National Front's 1988 defence statement endorsed European standardisation and conventional Franco-German cooperation. Paris can propose common specifications for selected equipment and supplier training, improving French access to components while retaining national command. The bargain requires German consent, education spending and acceptance of some outside influence over standards; it builds conventional interoperability without creating a joint force or transferring control of French equipment.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_gaullist_national_readiness: The 1970 reduction of active service to twelve months makes training and equipment standards central to the conscript army's readiness. This route keeps a large mechanised force available for a European emergency and gives priority to reinforcement and land doctrine. Such formations consume substantial supplies, so France must sustain transport, depots and exercises rather than treating conscript numbers alone as military strength.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_orthodox_force_de_dissuasion: France's force de frappe depends on secure command, trained naval crews and an industrial base able to maintain its submarines at home. This programme gives undersea expertise and dockyards priority, preserving the independent deterrent without claiming new weapons or delegated authority. The choice draws investment away from land arms production; national autonomy at sea requires long training cycles and a durable public commitment.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_liberal_professional_readine: A smaller professional establishment can preserve readiness by paying for maintainers, safety crews and trained specialists. Better care reduces supply waste and flying accidents, but a capable professional force costs more to retain than a large conscript reserve. This programme chooses dependable service and preparation over nominal size, and leaves the government responsible for sustaining the payroll through every procurement cycle.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_centre_civil_defence_service: The territorial engineer service joins military engineering with the roads, depots and civil-protection work needed during a national emergency. Training reservists in repair and logistics strengthens continuity beyond the standing army, but requires regular equipment, instructors and coordination with local services. France gains practical resilience rather than an expeditionary formation; the programme's value depends on keeping civilian infrastructure ready in peacetime.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_territorial_citizen_reserve: Republican territorial units can place reserve service under civilian oversight and prepare communities to defend local infrastructure. A broader reserve provides depth without building an expensive standing force, but initial training takes longer and readiness depends on employers releasing trained personnel. The policy makes home defence and parliamentary accountability the priority, accepting slower response from the professional army.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_socialist_citizen_reserve: The 1972 Common Programme proposed six-month service and trained regional reserves, pairing shorter conscription with democratic rights for soldiers and cadres. A socialist government can turn that promise into a territorial force with trained local units and a lighter standing payroll. Mobilisation depth improves, but specialist preparation takes longer and the system needs regional instructors, dependable employers and a clear route for career personnel.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_communist_party_command: A modern public armaments sector requires a trained general staff and technical schools capable of directing production, maintenance and supply. This programme concentrates expertise in national institutions rather than relying on foreign command or private contractors. Central coordination improves the state's ability to plan, but education and personnel carry a continuing cost, while regional units have less discretion over procurement priorities.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_old_guard_professional_staff: A hard-line French communist government can concentrate scarce specialists in a central staff and maintenance corps, ensuring public arsenals and field formations follow one plan. Professional expertise improves readiness and coordination but requires sustained pay and narrows the mass reserve's role. This central arrangement keeps production and command under Paris, but leaves local units less discretion and competes with wider service for skilled personnel.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_psu_citizen_defence: The PSU's later self-management current linked popular defence to civil service, territorial resilience and resistance to militarized society. A government could organize engineers, rescue services and local reserves around civilian authority, keeping strategic choices in French hands. This approach sacrifices central arms throughput and immediate expeditionary reach, while relying on local training and negotiated cooperation to protect communities and infrastructure.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_civil_protection_network: France's civil-protection services can coordinate rescue, engineering and emergency logistics without turning every public workshop into an arms plant. A territorial network improves repair capacity and limits supply demands, but requires trained personnel and regular local exercises. The programme protects communities and infrastructure rather than promising combat formations or overseas deployment, and its success depends on cooperation between national agencies and local authorities.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_territorial_readiness_compac: A lean standing establishment can keep French forces credible by extending equipment life and prioritising local maintenance. Lower personnel costs leave fewer trained replacements immediately available, so the army must accept slower reinforcement and depend on reserve employers. The arrangement suits a government seeking restraint in the regular payroll, but it cannot provide the rapid response of a larger professional force.
focus_descriptions.COLDWAR_FRA_national_service_reserve: A national service reserve can place territorial mobilisation ahead of an expensive professional establishment. The force draws on trained citizens and locally maintained equipment to defend French territory, but it takes longer to prepare than a specialist cadre. This route reflects the National Front's later emphasis on national defence as an alternate government policy, and leaves intervention beyond France's borders to a separate political decision.
